learningObjective: Apply Little's Law at the instruction/memory level to reason about the concurrency required to fully hide arithmetic and memory latency.

canonicalClaims.claim: GPU latency hiding requires enough outstanding operations (memory requests or independent instructions) to satisfy Little's Law; this concurrency can be provided by TLP (many warps), ILP (independent instructions per warp), or MLP (multiple outstanding loads per warp), and low-occupancy high-MLP kernels can still saturate memory bandwidth.
conditions: The kernel exposes independent operations that the scheduler can issue.
Sufficient hardware resources (LSU slots, functional units) exist to hold the concurrency.
nonImplications: Does not imply occupancy alone is sufficient; per-warp MLP/ILP matters.
Does not imply that any technique alone (TLP, ILP, MLP) works for every kernel; real kernels mix them.

misconceptions.whyWrong: If each active warp issues only a single outstanding load, aggregate concurrency may still fall short of BW × latency.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: Volkov 'Better Performance at Lower Occupancy' analysis

misconceptions.claim: Low occupancy always underutilizes the GPU.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Low-occupancy kernels with high per-warp MLP can saturate memory bandwidth; occupancy is only one way to reach the required concurrency.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: Volkov analysis; PMPP4 discussion of occupancy nuance

misconceptions.claim: ILP is irrelevant on GPUs; only TLP matters.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Warp schedulers issue instructions from a warp when its next instruction is ready; independent instructions within a warp allow issue without waiting on prior results.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide, warp scheduler semantics

implementationFacts: Little's Law: N (outstanding) = BW × latency; for A100 HBM ~ 800 KB in flight at 400 ns × 2 TB/s.
Warp scheduler issues one ready instruction per cycle from a warp; multiple warps + ILP + MLP jointly saturate the machine.
performanceScenarios: Reduction kernels are ILP-heavy per thread; matrix-transpose kernels are TLP-heavy across warps; MLP is a lever in memory-bound kernels.
